title: Associations of cerebrovascular resistance and endothelial function in cerebral small vessel disease affect postoperative neurocognitive outcome
summary:
Background
Older people may experience temporary confusion or changes in memory and thinking after surgery. It is not yet fully understood why some people are more vulnerable to these problems than others. The condition of the blood vessels, blood flow to the brain, the type of surgery and inflammatory processes in the body may play a role.

Research question
This study investigates whether simple examinations before surgery can help identify an increased risk of confusion or changes in memory and thinking after spinal surgery at an early stage. In the future, this could help provide better advice, monitoring and care for people at increased risk.

Methods
People aged 65 years or older who are scheduled for planned spinal surgery can take part. Before surgery, participants will complete questionnaires, a memory and attention test, an ultrasound examination of the blood vessels, an examination of blood vessel function in the arm and blood tests. After surgery, the hospital course, possible states of confusion, pain and routine treatment data will be documented. After three and six months, telephone follow-up interviews will assess memory, thinking and quality of life.
conditions: Delirium, not induced by alcohol and other psychoactive substances

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Planned elective spinal surgery without opening of the spinal dura mater
• Written informed consent after study information
• Sufficient language and cognitive abilities to perform the study assessments
Exclusion criteria:
• Moderate or severe dementia in the presence of a neurodegenerative disease
• Relevant psychiatric history
• CRP ≥ 50 mg/l or signs of active infection, for example fever
• Chronic use of centrally acting medication if it substantially affects neurocognitive assessment
• Active malignancy
• Medical or organizational reasons that make regular study participation, including follow-up assessments, impossible
